abstract: Precise camera control is essential for cinematic character video generation, yet existing methods struggle to follow large-angle trajectories with combined rotation, translation, and radius variation from arbitrary initial azimuths. Such viewpoint changes also reveal character regions unseen in the initial frame, causing geometric distortions, appearance degradation, and identity drift. To systematically study these coupled challenges, we introduce CLACT, a large-scale Character-centric dataset and benchmark covering diverse Large-Angle Camera Trajectories, with accurate camera geometry and multi-view character observations for training and evaluation. We further propose WorldCast, a framework for world-consistent character video generation under diverse large-angle camera motions. Specifically, we back-project the initial frame into a 3D point cloud using estimated depth, align the point-cloud scale with the target camera trajectory, and render it along the trajectory to obtain explicit geometric guidance and coverage masks. To complement the incomplete character information, we introduce Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention (GAMA). Using relative camera poses estimated jointly from the initial frame and multi-view character anchors, we express anchor and target-view geometry in a common coordinate frame. GAMA uses this geometric alignment to guide the retrieval and injection of view-relevant character features during generation. Evaluations across diverse large-angle camera trajectories demonstrate accurate trajectory following while preserving character geometry, appearance, and identity.

sections.body: The paper targets large-angle character camera control, where trajectories combine rotation, translation and radius change from arbitrary initial azimuths. It builds **CLACT**, which includes Unreal Engine 5 camera-motion sequences, Blender samples with multi-view character anchors, and an evaluation set of 42 scenes. It then proposes **WorldCast**, which couples scale-aligned geometric guidance with Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention (GAMA). The stated contributions are the dataset and benchmark, the WorldCast framework, and GAMA. The section states that the framework improves camera-control accuracy and cross-view character consistency while keeping competitive visual quality.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Large-angle camera motion couples trajectory accuracy with unseen character regions, so the paper introduces CLACT and WorldCast.

sections.body: Related work is grouped into three areas. Camera-controllable video generation covers methods such as MotionCtrl, CameraCtrl, UCPE and DualCamCtrl, along with video re-rendering methods. Geometry-aware and multi-view generation covers novel-view synthesis and explicit scene geometry for video. Identity-consistent generation covers subject-conditioned methods that preserve appearance across frames. The authors contrast these with their approach, which relates multi-view character-anchor geometry to the target trajectory so that view-relevant character evidence guides generation.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work covers camera-conditioned video, geometry-aware view synthesis, and identity-preserving generation, but not multi-view character anchors.

sections.body: The method builds on the flow-matching video backbone Wan2.1-I2V-14B. Depth for the initial frame comes from a pretrained estimator, and camera translation is rescaled over candidate scales. The chosen scale is the one whose rendered image motion best matches the reference video. The initial frame is back-projected into a colored point cloud and rendered along the trajectory, producing guidance frames and coverage masks that mark pixels the point cloud does not support. For GAMA, 20 memory-attention blocks are inserted after backbone blocks 0, 2, ..., 38. Video tokens retrieve character features from anchor tokens with shared camera encoding, and the residual is injected through zero-initialized projections. No limitations are stated in this section.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: WorldCast conditions a video diffusion backbone on projected geometric guidance and multi-view character memory through Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention.

sections.body: Training has two stages on Wan2.1-I2V-14B. Stage one uses rendered SpatialVID sequences plus UE5 sequences for camera control. Stage two trains GAMA on Blender samples with multi-view character anchors. The benchmark has 42 scenes, 17 synthetic and 25 real-world, each tested under six trajectories. In the main table, WorldCast reports ATE 0.065, relative translation error 0.020, relative rotation error 0.896, and MEt3R 0.228. These are the lowest values in each of those columns among all compared methods. Its image quality is 0.719, described as competitive. The authors note that additional reference views give limited or inconsistent gains for ViewCrafter and MVGenMaster.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On 42 scenes, WorldCast reaches the lowest absolute trajectory error of 0.065 among compared methods.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes CLACT and WorldCast as a dataset, benchmark and framework for large-angle camera-controlled video generation. It credits the combination of scale-aligned geometric guidance with GAMA for more accurate camera control and stronger preservation of character geometry, appearance and identity, while visual quality stays competitive. The ablation studies are cited for large-angle training data, explicit camera-ray conditioning, geometric anchor alignment and multi-view character memory. Stated future work covers more flexible anchor acquisition, more complex dynamic scenes, and longer or interactive camera trajectories, which the paper does not address.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Ablations attribute gains to large-angle training data, camera-ray conditioning, anchor alignment and multi-view memory, while dynamic scenes remain future work.

sections.body: The appendix begins with generative tool use, ethics and reproducibility statements. Appendix A describes depth-trajectory scale calibration. Pixel motion from rendered and reference videos is compared across candidate scales, using tracks from pyramidal Lucas-Kanade optical flow, up to 1200 corners per frame pair, and a 3-pixel RANSAC threshold. Appendix B describes UE5 and Blender data construction, with 99 characters and 33 environments. Appendix C defines benchmark protocols and metrics. Appendix D reports an anchor-routing analysis in which 19 of the 21 latent positions agree, plus extra qualitative results. The ethics statement discourages deceptive depictions of real individuals without consent.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers scale calibration, data construction, metric protocols and extra analyses, after ethics and reproducibility statements.
